report_html:
Ground mismatch: BAL are run-first (30% pass when leading) into a NO front that bleeds 132 rush yds/game and 0.68 RB1 rushing scores. Derrick Henry is a centerpiece — and the game script only feeds him.

The BAL host the NO as favorites of 7.5, with the total set at 46.5 — a market that implies a BAL 27–20 scoreline. Running the game forward from that baseline, we expect a contest that spends roughly 39% of its snaps with BAL in front, 35% within one score, and 26% with BAL chasing. That distribution is the engine of everything below: game state is what turns a team's tendencies into a specific player's workload, so before we get to individuals it's worth being explicit about how this game is likely to be played.

This projects as a game BAL should control. A favorite of 8 sits in front for the majority of the second half in most simulations, which pulls the script toward the run and clock management for BAL and toward volume passing and tempo for NO, who will be throwing to keep pace. Expect NO to run more total plays than BAL — trailing teams go no-huddle (league no-huddle rate climbs from ~8% in neutral game states to over 20% when down two scores), and that extra volume is a tailwind for NO's pass-catchers even in a losing effort.

The Key Matchups

BAL's outside-zone run game (33% to the edge) attacks a leaky NO front — chunk-run upside for Derrick Henry.

Tough sledding for Travis Etienne — BAL are stingy against the run (94 yds/game, well below the ~120 norm); lean under on his rushing line.

Tyler Shough has a passing-yards tailwind — BAL allow 257 pass yds/game (vs ~230).

Chris Olave draws a plus matchup — BAL concede 74 yds/game to WR1s (league ~58). A rec-yards spot.

Travis Etienne eats as a receiver too — BAL give up 22 rec yds/game to backs, and NO target the RB on 20% of throws.

Zay Flowers faces a tough cover — NO hold WR1s to just 51 yds/game (vs ~58); a rec-yards under lean.

Touchdown Board

Derrick Henry is a bell-cow (76% of carries) meeting a defense that allows 0.68 RB rushing TDs/game — strong anytime-TD equity.

Zay Flowers carries TD equity — NO surrender 0.47 WR1 receiving scores a game.

Game Script, Pace & Environment

Script leans BAL. As a 8-point favorite they project to lead much of the game, tilting toward the run late — Derrick Henry's carry ceiling rises in the blowout branches. Meanwhile NO throw to keep pace, a volume tailwind for Chris Olave.

A middling 46 total — no strong lean either way; the value is in the individual matchups above, not the game environment.

BAL — a run-heavy offense

BAL are one of the league's more run-committed offenses: on early downs while leading, they pass just 30% of the time, against a league average of 44% — a genuine clock-bleeding identity, not noise (it holds after shrinking their sample toward the league).

This is the profile that most rewards a lead back. As a 8-point favorite projected to lead for 39% of snaps, BAL will be running to close the game, and their run-first identity compounds it. Derrick Henry is the beneficiary — we project 16 carries for 77 yards, and his ceiling is where the value sits: in the simulations where this becomes a two-score game, his volume spikes as BAL salt it away.

The flip side: Zay Flowers (6 targets, 57 yards) has his ceiling capped by the same script that helps the run game — when BAL lead and run, there simply aren't as many pass attempts to go around. He's a safer floor than ceiling play in this spot.

Underneath, Mark Andrews (TE, 3 targets, 28 yards) is the dependable secondary read — and note the red zone stays TE-friendly regardless of score, so his touchdown equity holds up even if the game script shifts.

NO — a run-heavy offense

NO are one of the league's more run-committed offenses: on early downs while leading, they pass just 37% of the time, against a league average of 44% — a genuine clock-bleeding identity, not noise (it holds after shrinking their sample toward the league).

Game script works against the run here — NO project to trail and throw, which squeezes Travis Etienne's rushing projection (14 carries, 59 yards) but raises his value as a receiver; trailing teams check the ball down, and his target share ticks up as the game gets away from them.

Chris Olave is the one to target from a volume standpoint: as underdogs throwing to keep pace, NO funnel work to their top receiver — 10 targets for 82 yards projected, with genuine upside if they fall behind early and the game turns one-dimensional.

Underneath, Juwan Johnson (TE, 5 targets, 38 yards) is the dependable secondary read — and note the red zone stays TE-friendly regardless of score, so his touchdown equity holds up even if the game script shifts.

What to watch

The single biggest swing factor is availability — use the injury tool in the sidebar to mark anyone out; a starter's absence doesn't just remove his line, it redistributes his targets and carries to specific teammates, and the report and projections rebuild around it. Beyond that: if this game breaks toward the projected 8-point margin, the garbage-time backups (the ◆-flagged rows below) are where soft lines and real edge tend to appear — those depth players get fed in blowouts, and the market is slowest to price them.

This preview and the projections below regenerate through the week as injuries, weather and line moves update the inputs.
